title: How do the French inform themselves on the Internet? Analysis of online information and disinformation behaviors (Fondation Descartes, March 2021)
screen_reason: Behavioural panel-trace study (Respondi French Access panel, N = 2,372, 30 days of complete web/app/YouTube tracking) in which 2,946 French-language information sources were classified reliable vs unreliable (Storyzy algorithm, validated against Le Monde's Decodex, Cohen's kappa = 0.896). The report gives the share of panellists who visited an unreliable source at least once (REACH) and the share of information time and of total connected time spent on unreliable sources (EXPOSURE), plus per-category reach for generic disinformation, health disinformation and click-bait.

estimates.platform: All web and mobile-app traffic on participants' personal devices, incl. associated Facebook/Twitter pages and YouTube channels
estimates.measure_type: % of tracked panellists who visited at least one information source classified unreliable during the 30-day period
estimates.denominator: 2,372 members of Respondi's French Access panel, representative of the French population aged 18+, whose complete internet activity was recorded for 30 days
estimates.definition: Participant recorded as having consulted (visited a URL of, or a mobile app / associated Facebook or Twitter page / YouTube channel of) at least one of the tracked information sources that Storyzy's algorithm classified as unreliable
estimates.misinfo_def: "Generic disinformation. These are the sources deemed unreliable by Storyzy that provide information and news content on principally political and social topics. These domains are considered to be unreliable because at least some of the published content contributes to conspiracy theories or consists of false information."
estimates.source_quote: Among all participants (N = 2,372), time spent consulting information sources deemed unreliable corresponds to 5% of total connected time dedicated to information, or 0.16% of total connected time. However, not all participants consulted such sources during the study's 30-day period. Indeed, only 39% of participants consulted information sources considered to be unreliable.
estimates.page_loc: Section 3.6.1, p. 26 (also stated in Key Findings p. 5 and Discussion p. 36)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Storyzy commercial algorithm classified all 2,946 tracked sources binary reliable/unreliable on the basis of relations between domains (authors, links, citations, content reuse) seeded by manual evaluation; the authors then visited each unreliable source to assign its main topic. Cross-validated on the 366 sources also rated by Le Monde's Decodex fact-checkers: Cohen's kappa = 0.896.
estimates.moderator_quote: The binary categorization proposed by Storyzy (i.e., reliable and unreliable) was applied to all of the sources tracked in this study. ... From this statistical analysis, it appears that the consistency between the Decodex and Storyzy categorizations on this common sample of 366 websites is excellent (Cohen's kappa = 0.896).
estimates.notes: Whole-panel figure (N = 2,372), the report's headline reach number, repeated verbatim in the Key Findings and the Discussion. Denominator is who was tracked, hence denom_scope = population. 'Unreliable' here pools generic disinformation, health disinformation, click-bait, pseudoscience and satire.

estimates.measure_type: % of tracked panellists who visited at least one source of generic (political/social) disinformation during the 30-day period

estimates.definition: Visited at least once, over 30 days, a tracked source classified unreliable by Storyzy whose main topic the authors judged to be political/social news ('generic disinformation')

These domains are considered to be unreliable because at least some of the published content contributes to conspiracy theories or consists of false information."
estimates.source_quote: Lastly, it is interesting to note that only 9.4% of all study participants visited sources of generic disinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Storyzy algorithmic domain-reliability list (cross-validated against Decodex, kappa = 0.896); the authors then visited every unreliable source themselves to assign it to exactly one topical category, of which 'generic disinformation' is the political/social one.
estimates.moderator_quote: After having visited each of the sources considered to be unreliable, we identified the principal topic of each of these sources. We thus arrived at the following classification of information sources considered to be unreliable: generic disinformation, health-related disinformation, "click-bait," pseudoscience and satire.
estimates.notes: Narrower definitional variant of the 39% row (political/social disinformation sources only), hence definition_variant = true. The Discussion figure over the whole panel (9.4% of 2,372) is preferred to the Results figure over survey completers only (Section 3.6.1: '163 (10.1%)' of the 1,614 who finished the end-of-study survey) because it shares the denominator of the 39% headline; both are verbatim.

estimates.platform: All web and mobile-app traffic on participants' personal devices, incl. associated Facebook/Twitter pages and YouTube channels
estimates.measure_type: % of surveyed panellists who visited at least one 'click-bait' source during the 30-day period
estimates.value_raw: 491 (30.4%) of 1,614 participants visited a source of "click-bait" at least once
estimates.denominator: 1,614 of the 2,372 tracked panellists — those who also completed the end-of-study survey
estimates.definition: Visited at least once, over 30 days, a tracked source classified unreliable by Storyzy and assigned to the 'click-bait' category
estimates.misinfo_def: "Click-bait. These are the sources deemed unreliable and considered to belong to the "click-bait" category by Storyzy. "Click-bait" sources are those whose content is not intended to inform the reader, but solely to attract their attention in order to generate traffic on their page. "Click-bait" sources employ various deceptive methods: intentionally shocking or sensationalist titles, content that does not correspond to the title of an article, off-topic or falsified header images, etc."
estimates.source_quote: Of the 1,614 participants who complete the end-of-study survey, 491 (30.4%) visited a source of “click-bait” at least once.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Storyzy algorithmic domain-reliability list, click-bait sub-category (cross-validated against Decodex on the reliable/unreliable split, kappa = 0.896).
estimates.moderator_quote: "Click-bait" sources employ various deceptive methods: intentionally shocking or sensationalist titles, content that does not correspond to the title of an article, off-topic or falsified header images, etc.
estimates.notes: borderline = true: click-bait is coded as deceptive/misleading rather than false, so the numerator can include sources whose individual articles are not untrue. It is nevertheless inside the paper's 'unreliable' set and inside the 39% headline row, and by volume it is 41% of all unreliable time. Kept as the broadest definitional variant; an adjudicator may prefer to treat it as QUALITY-adjacent and drop it. breadth = misleading on the strength of the 'deceptive methods' definition.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Composition of misinformation exposure (Fig. 26): of the time the 921 consulters spent on unreliable sources, 43% was on generic disinformation, 41% click-bait, 14% health disinformation, 2% pseudoscience, <1% satire. Not extracted as prevalence rows — the denominator is unreliable-source time itself, so these describe the internal mix of misinformation exposure, not its prevalence (would be within_misinfo_content rows at best). 2) Conditional intensity among the exposed: the 39% who consulted unreliable sources spent on average 40 seconds/day (median 7 s) on them, '10.9% of their daily connected time dedicated to information (median = 3.7%), or 0.4% of their total connected time'. Not extracted: the denominator is restricted to the exposed subgroup, which is not a population prevalence. 3) Concentration-like numbers are all about news consumption in general, not misinformation: 'The 26 online information sources that were most consulted constitute 40% of the time spent consuming information on the Internet' (top-26 of 1,290 sources actually consulted / 2,946 tracked). No CONCENTRATION row written — the review's concentration construct concerns misinformation exposure or sharing, and conc_group_pct would have to be computed from an ambiguous source denominator. 4) Heavy-tail statements without a share: 'the 20 participants who consulted them the most did so for an average of 4 hours' and 'about 10 participants to our study spent a total of more than two and a half hours on sources of generic disinformation' — bare counts of accounts, unusable under R1. 5) Echo-chamber figure '68% of these participants also consulted the online source of a traditional nation-wide media outlet at least once' — a reliable-media share, not a misinformation share. 6) Section 3.6.1 also gives 163 (10.1%) of 1,614 survey completers for generic disinformation; the 9.4%-of-2,372 whole-panel figure was preferred for the row. 7) Demographic subgroup contrasts (e.g. health-disinfo consulters 56% women vs 48%) not extracted per the subgroup rule. 8) No self-report exposure share is reported: the end-of-study survey covered sources consulted and trust, and the reported-vs-effective comparison is correlational, so no RECALL row exists.

rob.design: Behavioural passive-metering panel: 2,372 members of Respondi's French Access panel, assembled to be representative of the French population aged 18+, tracked across computer, tablet and phone for 30 consecutive days (20 Sep - 19 Oct 2020); only 48% consented to phone tracking in addition to other devices and 24% were phone-only. 2,946 French-language sources tracked (2,295 websites with their apps/Facebook/Twitter/YouTube channels, plus 651 independent YouTube channels), all with >=15,000 monthly visitors/subscribers. Source reliability from Storyzy's relational algorithm, not per-item coding; agreement with Le Monde's Decodex fact-checkers on the 366 overlapping sources was Cohen's kappa = 0.896. Time recording paused after 3 minutes of inactivity. End-of-study survey completed by 1,614 of 2,372 (68%). Acknowledged blind spots: foreign-language sources, non-personal devices, and news read inside Facebook walls / Twitter feeds or private groups without clicking through.
